content.title: Lubricants
content.description: Lubricants are substances introduced between two moving surfaces to reduce friction, wear, heat generation, and energy loss while ensuring smooth operation of machines.

content.content: Lubrication is an essential process in mechanical and industrial systems. A lubricant forms a protective film between moving parts, preventing direct metal-to-metal contact. Besides reducing friction, lubricants also help in cooling, cleaning, corrosion prevention, sealing, and increasing the life of machine components.

Depending on operating conditions such as load, speed, and temperature, different types of lubricants and lubrication mechanisms are employed in automobiles, turbines, compressors, bearings, gears, engines, and heavy industrial machinery.

content.title: Engineering Importance
content.content: Proper lubrication reduces maintenance cost, improves efficiency, minimizes power loss, prevents wear, and increases the service life of machines.
Functions of Lubricants

A lubricant performs several important functions such as reducing friction between moving surfaces, minimizing wear and tear, carrying away heat, preventing corrosion, reducing noise, sealing gaps between moving parts, and protecting machinery from rust and oxidation.

items.question: Reduce Friction
items.answer: Prevents direct contact between moving surfaces.

items.question: Cooling
items.answer: Removes heat generated due to friction.

items.question: Corrosion Protection
items.answer: Protects metal surfaces from oxidation and rust.

items.question: Cleaning
items.answer: Carries away dirt, carbon particles, and wear debris.

content.content: Classification of Lubricants
Lubricants are classified mainly into liquid, semi-solid, solid, and gaseous lubricants depending on their physical state and applications.

content.title: Examples
content.content: Engine oil is a liquid lubricant, grease is a semi-solid lubricant, graphite and molybdenum disulphide (MoS₂) are solid lubricants, while air acts as a gaseous lubricant.
Characteristics of a Good Lubricant

A good lubricant should possess suitable viscosity, high flash and fire points, low volatility, good oxidation stability, high oiliness, low pour point, resistance to corrosion, and should maintain its lubricating properties over a wide temperature range.

items.question: Low Pour Point
items.answer: Allows flow even at low temperatures.

items.question: High Oiliness
items.answer: Provides strong adhesion to metal surfaces.

content.content: Mechanism of Lubrication

Lubrication mechanisms depend on the thickness of the lubricant film formed between moving surfaces. The three important mechanisms are thick film lubrication, thin film lubrication, and extreme pressure lubrication.
Thick Film (Hydrodynamic) Lubrication

In thick film lubrication, a thick layer of lubricant completely separates the moving surfaces. Since there is no direct metal-to-metal contact, friction and wear are very low. This mechanism is commonly observed in high-speed and lightly loaded machines.

content.title: Applications
content.content: Used in turbines, electric motors, centrifugal pumps, and journal bearings.
Thin Film (Boundary) Lubrication

Thin film lubrication occurs when only a very thin molecular layer of lubricant exists between moving surfaces. The lubricant molecules adhere strongly to the metal surfaces and reduce friction under moderate load and low-speed conditions.

content.title: Applications
content.content: Common in gears, machine tools, automobile engines during starting, and reciprocating machines.
Extreme Pressure Lubrication

Extreme pressure lubrication is used when machines operate under very high load and temperature. Special additives containing sulphur, phosphorus, or chlorine react chemically with metal surfaces to form a protective layer that prevents welding and severe wear.

content.title: Applications
content.content: Used in heavy-duty gears, cutting tools, rolling mills, mining equipment, and high-load industrial machinery.
Comparison of Lubrication Mechanisms

content.content: Properties of Lubricants

The quality of a lubricant is evaluated by several physical properties such as viscosity, cloud point, pour point, flash point, and fire point. These properties determine its suitability for different operating conditions.
Viscosity
Viscosity is the internal resistance offered by a lubricant to flow. It is the most important property because it determines the thickness of the lubricating film formed between moving surfaces.
Cloud Point
Cloud point is the temperature at which wax crystals first begin to separate from the lubricant, giving it a cloudy appearance during cooling.
Pour Point
Pour point is the lowest temperature at which a lubricant is capable of flowing under specified conditions. Lubricants used in cold regions should possess a low pour point.
Flash Point
Flash point is the lowest temperature at which lubricant vapours ignite momentarily when exposed to a flame. It indicates the safety of the lubricant during storage and operation.
Fire Point
Fire point is the minimum temperature at which the lubricant continues to burn for at least five seconds after ignition. It is always higher than the flash point.
Applications of Lubricants

items.question: Automobile Industry
items.answer: Engine oils, gear oils, brake systems, and transmission units.

items.question: Power Plants
items.answer: Lubrication of turbines, generators, and compressors.

items.question: Manufacturing Industry
items.answer: Machine tools, bearings, conveyors, and hydraulic systems.

items.question: Aerospace
items.answer: Aircraft engines and precision mechanical components.

items.question: Marine Industry
items.answer: Ship engines, propeller shafts, and heavy-duty gears.

Extreme pressure lubrication uses chemically active additives.

Pour point is the lowest temperature at which oil flows.
Flash point is the ignition temperature of vapours.
Fire point is the temperature for continuous burning.
Lubricants improve machine efficiency and service life.
